name: Battle of Shanghai
note: This plan shows the whole operation, not a single field: each block is an army, a corps or a fleet, and the towns, creeks and the river are the ground it was fought over. The accounts give only rough directions and distances, so the positions are schematic. Many Chinese and Japanese divisions are folded into the formations the accounts name most often; the accounts do not say which Japanese divisions stood where at each date.

phases.title: The first Chinese attack is halted
phases.text: The 88th Division attacked the Japanese positions in downtown Shanghai in the late afternoon. Direct fire from the entrenched Japanese and bombardment by the Third Fleet in the Huangpu halted it.
phases.quote: the Chinese 88th Division attacked Japanese positions in downtown Shanghai, but was halted by direct fire from the entrenched Japanese and heavy bombardments from the Japanese Third Fleet moored in the Huangpu.

phases.title: Operation Iron Fist
phases.text: The 88th and 87th Divisions shelled the Japanese positions and then charged with infantry. Poor coordination between infantry and artillery and the shelling from the ships kept them from a major breakthrough, and by 18 August the attack was called off.
phases.quote: the 88th and 87th Divisions launched Iron Fist, first intensely shelling the Japanese positions and then charging with infantry.

phases.title: The 36th Division attacks towards the docks
phases.text: The newly arrived 36th Division was sent in on 19 August, half of it towards the Hueishan docks on the northern side of the Huangpu, to cut the Japanese forces in two. It fought through the streets under fire from the buildings and from the Third Fleet.
phases.quote: On August 19, two regiments of the 36th Division began their assault towards the wharf, enduring withering fire from Japanese defenders positioned on the roofs and upper floors of the buildings lining the streets.

phases.title: Chinese tanks reach Broadway but the wharf holds
phases.text: The Japanese were pushed back towards the docks, and by 21 August Chinese tanks had reached Broadway, the last street before the Huangpu. The Japanese held the high walls of the wharf and the Chinese could not finish the breakthrough.
phases.quote: By August 21, 1937, Chinese tanks had managed to punch through to Broadway, the last street before the Huangpu.

phases.title: Japanese troops land on the coast
phases.text: The Japanese 3rd and 11th Divisions landed on the north-east coast under naval bombardment, and the Chinese brought troops from the city to meet them. The front line was lengthened from the city to the coast.
phases.quote: the Japanese 3rd and 11th Divisions made an amphibious assault under the cover of naval bombardment and proceeded to land

phases.title: Baoshan falls
phases.text: Chinese troops held the walled town of Baoshan against several Japanese assaults. The Japanese surrounded it, a tank assault with air support broke through the gate, and the town fell on 6 September.
phases.quote: On the next day, September 6, 1937, Baoshan fell.

phases.title: The fight for Luodian
phases.text: The Chinese concentrated around Luodian and the Japanese came inland against them with naval gunfire, tanks and aircraft. The Chinese were bled almost dry and gave up the town by the end of September.
phases.quote: To defend Luodian, the Chinese concentrated some 300,000 soldiers there, while the Japanese amassed more than 100,000 troops

phases.title: Liujiahang and Gujiazhai fall
phases.text: The Japanese 3rd Division attacked the Liujiahang and Gujiazhai positions on the right wing of the Chinese group army, while the 11th Division pursued it. After days of attacks and counterattacks the Chinese retreated.
phases.quote: On October 1, Liujiahang was occupied by the 34th Infantry Regiment. The next day, the 8th and 16th Divisions also retreated, and the Japanese army occupied Gujiazhai.

phases.title: The Japanese reach the Wusong Creek
phases.text: The Chinese fell back to the south bank of the Wusong Creek, and the Japanese attacked across it. The line was breached after two days at one bridge, but the Japanese met further defences behind it.
phases.quote: On October 5, 1937, the Japanese forces smashed into the Chinese defenses across the Wusong Creek

phases.title: The Guangxi counteroffensive
phases.text: The Guangxi Army joined the line and counterattacked to retake the banks of the creek. It was poorly coordinated and bogged down, and the Japanese answered with artillery, tanks and poison gas.
phases.quote: These Guangxi units, four divisions in total, then staged a final counteroffensive on October 21

phases.title: Dachang falls and the Chinese leave the city
phases.text: The Japanese pushed on to Dachang and took it. The Chinese then withdrew from downtown Shanghai, which they had held for almost three months, to a line behind the Suzhou Creek.
phases.quote: The fighting continued until October 26, when Dachang finally fell.

phases.title: The Sihang Warehouse is held
phases.text: A battalion of the 88th Division, some 411 men under Xie Jinyuan, made a stand in the Sihang Warehouse on the Suzhou Creek. Its thick walls and the nearness of the International Settlement nullified Japanese firepower, and several attacks were beaten back.
phases.quote: Between October 27 and November 1, 1937, the 1st Battalion defended Sihang Warehouse against multiple attacks from the Japanese.

phases.title: The Japanese cross the Suzhou Creek
phases.text: On 30 October the Japanese crossed the Suzhou Creek, and the Chinese troops were in danger of encirclement. The Japanese 3rd Division began landing on the east side of the creek on 31 October.
phases.quote: On October 30, the Japanese crossed Suzhou River and the Chinese troops were in danger of encirclement.

phases.title: The 10th Army lands at Jinshanwei
phases.text: On 5 November the Japanese 10th Army, made up of units diverted from the Battle of Taiyuan, landed at Jinshanwei on Hangzhou Bay, a position held by only two companies of the 63rd Division.
phases.quote: to land easily in Jinshanwei on November 5, 1937
